articles.title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport
articles.summary: Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
articles.body: Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight. Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.” During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed. Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. “We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.” It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.” The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.” The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.” Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition. “The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.” Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said.

articles.title: Three killed, one injured in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say

articles.title: The boy making all the right moves in India’s chess revolution
articles.summary: The lights were out. A thunderstorm had cut the power. But 8-year-old Tamizh Amudhan had a chess match to play against one of the best players in the world.
articles.body: The lights were out. A thunderstorm had cut the power. But 8-year-old Tamizh Amudhan had a chess match to play against one of the best players in the world. By the flicker of a candle, he sat on the floor of his family home in southern India, his laptop balanced on a pillow and its battery draining fast. Still, the boy played on, pulling off a stunning upset against German grandmaster Vincent Keymer, then ranked world No. 7. It was the kind of opportunity Tamizh might never have had if his parents hadn’t made a life-changing decision two years earlier. In 2024, they left behind the stability of life in their hometown and moved to Sivakasi, a small town in India’s Tamil Nadu state, the epicenter of the country’s chess boom. There, they have restructured their lives around one dream: that Tamizh becomes the greatest chess player in the world. The head coach at Hatsun Chess Academy in Sivakasi, where Tamizh now studies full-time, believes the boy possesses the rare gift of an instinctive understanding of the chessboard that is extraordinarily difficult to teach. “He has unique tendencies to see long lines of geometry,” Vishnu Prasanna told CNN, in a classroom with some of India’s most promising young chess players. “Not easy to teach a kid his age.” Indians have long been celebrated for producing mathematical minds, spelling bee champions and tech talent that has helped shape Silicon Valley. Now, in the nation of 1.4 billion people, a new generation is emerging, producing grandmasters, record-breakers and world title contenders at a rapid pace. One face of this boom is grandmaster Gukesh Dommaraju, who stunned the chess world in 2024 by becoming the youngest world champion in history at 18 after beating China’s Ding Liren. Beginning Tuesday, November 24, Gukesh will be defending his title at the World Chess Championship in Geneva. Five-time world champion and current world No. 1, Norwegian grandmaster Magnus Carlsen told CNN he is not surprised that India is the “best chess country in the world.” “India has both the biggest numbers in terms of youth players and chess fans. It’s been incredible to see the boom that has happened there,” he said. “I think it’s only going to get better from here.” Sivakasi is best known as India’s fireworks capital, producing around 90% of the country’s firecrackers and other pyro products. But in a place more accustomed to making things explode in the sky, a quieter kind of revolution is underway. Chess schools have popped up in Sivakasi and around the state, including Hatsun Chess Academy, the country’s first residential training center for the sport. Children arrive at the academy in the early hours of the morning, trundling out of buses and auto-rickshaws that bump along the rugged roads. They race into the class, beaming and eager to start the day. The one and only subject at this academy is chess. For other subjects, Tamizh is homeschooled by his mother. Vishnu, the academy’s head coach, knows something about developing prodigious talent. He coached Gukesh during his formative years, giving him firsthand experience of what it takes for an exceptional young player to reach the top. Now he is trying to create an environment where that serious training can begin even earlier. “You’re supposed to become much stronger at a very young age,” Vishnu said. “Top players in chess have put academics in the background.” Some 50 students are currently enrolled in the academy. From Monday to Friday, they work through drills designed to sharpen their calculation skills, repeatedly solving positions and plotting moves. They also engage in simulated tournaments. Entry to the academy is fiercely competitive. Earning a place here can be almost as challenging as the training itself. Students must be ranked among the top 30 nationally in their age group to apply. Selected candidates then undergo a month of provisional training where coaches assess whether they are ready to join full time. The academy says it receives up to 40 applications monthly, but most don’t make the cut. For selected children, the path demands an unusual degree of focus at an early age. It is a world of endless possibilities on the chessboard but one that leaves less room for a typical childhood. Marium Fatima, 19, moved more than 1,000 miles from her home in India’s Bihar state to Sivakasi to achieve her dream of becoming a grandmaster. “Coming from Bihar, chess is not a sport which is developed yet,” she said. But at the academy, she said she is able to compete against “many strong players” and learn how they approach the game. “There’s a bit of family time that I miss,” she said. “I have to endure that if I want to improve my chess.” Vishnu acknowledged that specializing so young comes with some disadvantages. But he says the academy is doing more than gunning for grandmasters. “We believe that we are building personalities,” he said. “You can consider this as an investment rather than a huge risk.” Few understand the sacrifices better than Viswanathan Anand. Nicknamed the “Lightning Kid” for the speed of his play, and later the “Tiger of Madras,” for his savage attack, Anand became India’s first grandmaster in 1988, followed by its first world champion 12 years later, setting the stage for a generation of Indian players who believed that they, too, could compete at the top. “It did feel special in those days. Every time I did something, it was for the first time by an Indian. In many cases, first time by a nation,” the 56-year-old grandmaster told CNN. He admits that none of it would have been possible if not for the sacrifices his mother made, accompanying him from tournament to tournament. “I always say that behind every one of India’s great players is one exhausted parent,” Anand said. “That kind of dedication and support means a lot.” Tamizh picked up the game by watching his older cousins play, and by the time he was four, his parents began to wonder whether their son had an unusual talent. Tamizh seemed convinced of it too, when he begged them to let him enter a district-level tournament. His father, Sathish A., said no because the competition would involve older kids, and he didn’t want his son to be embarrassed. “He repeatedly asked for permission and I repeatedly refused,” Sathish said. The government worker says he doesn’t consider himself much of a chess player but has a knack for mathematics and was the ninth top student in his civil exams. Eventually, the father decided to put his son to the test. The two had a showdown. Tamizh, then 4, beat his father, 32. “After that, we decided to let him play,” Sathish said. Among the audience at the small district competition was a bus conductor who was also a chess coach. He saw something special in the boy and offered to train him for free. His parents took up the offer. Early in Tamizh’s chess journey, the family struggled to cover the cost of traveling to tournaments to refine his skills. There was much relief in 2024 when Tamizh received a scholarship to the Hatsun Chess Academy. However, it meant the family was split up for more than a year. Tamizh moved with his mother, Uma K., to Sivakasi while his father stayed at home with his sister in Kallakurichi, some 220 miles away. Twice a month, mother and son would travel to tournaments, sometimes journeying through the night in a country where traveling alone can carry risks for women. “It’s lonely and difficult, but (Tamizh) has managed everything,” Uma said. “He never says he is too tired or that he doesn’t want training, these are words that never come out of his mouth.” A family divided by distance was emotionally taxing for everyone, but Tamizh’s father left his job and took a new one in October to be closer to his son. “Risks and sacrifices are something every parent makes for their kid,” Sathish said. “Within six months at the academy, Tamizh achieved what would usually take four years… He’s able to produce such results, so I never had any doubt.” Chess is widely believed to trace its roots to 6th-century India, where an early version of the game, Chaturanga, mirrored the battlefield: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots; pieces that would evolve into the pawn, knight, bishop and rook. For decades, Russia and the United States produced its biggest champions. But now, the country where the story began is emerging as a force yet again. India’s growing chess prowess was on display in June at a major international tournament in Hong Kong, with young fans lining up to get a glimpse of their favorite stars. Among the slew of top Indian players taking part was Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, known simply as Pragg, one of the most recognizable faces in the chess scene. Adding further excitement to the event was Arjun Erigaisi who defeated Norwegian legend Carlsen in the sixth round of the rapid competition, helping his team advance to the next round. “Anything less than first place when India competes in a tournament is seen as a disappointment,” said Erigaisi’s team captain Srinath Narayan. “That’s how much chess has changed in India in the last 20 years.” Besides producing more talent, India’s spellbound chess moves are creating opportunities for big bucks too. India’s Global Chess League (GCL), the world’s first rapid chess league, was launched in 2023 by the International Chess Federation and Indian multinational firm Tech Mahindra. It is modeled after cricket’s massive Indian Premier League, which is estimated to be worth $20 billion in the cricket-mad nation. Top names in the chess world, including Carlsen, play in the league. For Anand Mahindra, chairperson of Indian conglomerate Mahindra & Mahindra and the mastermind behind the league, this moment has been years in the making. India’s extraordinary pipeline of chess talent, he said, is “no longer a coincidence.” “The first ecosystem produced champions,” Mahindra told CNN from his office in Mumbai. “I think the real opportunity now is to create a chess culture all across India.” The billionaire businessman is betting on chess developing to be an attractive spectator sport. The league’s latest season in September racked up more than 250,000 viewing hours on chess.com, the sport’s largest online platform. “Ultimately, sport is about human emotion,” Mahindra said. “The untapped potential… is really to unleash the human drama that chess has within it when it’s played as a team sport.” There is little on the road to Tamizh’s new home in Sivakasi to suggest that one of India’s most promising young chess players is growing up there. Inside their modest three-bedroom house, the now nine-year-old lives with his parents and 10-year-old sister. Tamizh’s parents say they’ve never worried that chess is taking up too much of his time. Sitting in their living room, surrounded by his trophies, they say their chess-obsessed son constantly works on his game. “Instead of being worried, I’d say I’m proud,” Sathish said. Tamizh wasn’t able to articulate exactly why he loves chess so much but his passion was clear. “It’s very jolly to play,” he said. He pointed out that he has no interest in video games or television shows. “I enjoy the academy more,” he said. “Everything is jolly and we can play (chess).” Hopes are high for little Tamizh to fully unleash his potential. While others painstakingly strategize to become better players, Tamizh’s gameplan is simple – but effective. “There is no strategy. I just play normally,” he said with a cheeky smile. “When you see your opponent, you should not have fear.” Tamizh admits there are things he misses about his old hometown: his friends, his relatives, and a life that perhaps felt a little more carefree. “Being there is a bit jollier than here,” he said. But there is a reason he is here. “I want to play even better.” How much better? Tamizh has an answer for that, too. “In everything I want to be the world’s youngest,” he said. “The world’s youngest grandmaster, I can do that in one year. The youngest world champion, I can do it in two.”

articles.title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
articles.summary: "Just accept Brexit and move on," the former prime minister tells BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.
articles.body:
Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.

At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.

In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023 , she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?

Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says

UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns

On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.

Speaking to The Sunday Times , Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme .

The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

articles.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.summary: At least three people were killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory.
articles.body:
At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

articles.title: Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
articles.summary: Behind Somalia’s break with the UAE lies a domestic power struggle with regional leaders close to Abu Dhabi.
articles.body:
Three years ago, at a town hall meeting in Mogadishu, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud defended one of his country’s most controversial foreign partnerships.

The United Arab Emirates, he declared, was “one of the greatest pillars” of Somalia’s war against the al-Qaeda-linked armed group al-Shabab. He praised Abu Dhabi’s support for the country’s armed forces despite longstanding concerns about its political influence.

Having returned to power in 2022, Mohamud sought to repair relations with the Gulf state after a period of strained ties under his predecessor, while reassuring a sceptical Somali public that the UAE’s involvement was a boon rather than a hindrance.

This year, that relationship unravelled spectacularly.

On November 19, Somalia ordered the Emirati ambassador to leave the country and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, marking the sharpest rupture yet in a relationship that had shifted from close security cooperation and deep commercial ties to open hostility.

The UAE said it had already withdrawn its diplomatic staff from Mogadishu in January.

The decision came 10 months after Somalia annulled several commercial, defence and security agreements with the UAE, accusing its former ally of undermining its sovereignty.

In a sharp public rebuke two days before the expulsion order, Mohamud accused the UAE of heightening political divisions, financing rival regional administrations and supporting armed actors operating beyond the federal government’s control.

“A brother does not burn your house. A brother does not buy your property without your knowledge. A brother does not divide your family,” he said.

“After years of diplomatic engagement, the Federal Government assesses that UAE policies threaten Somalia’s national security,” Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, Somalia’s national security adviser (NSA), said in a post on X.

The UAE hit back, accusing Mogadishu of allowing its internal political disputes to strain bilateral ties, in an apparent reference to the president’s contentious relations with some of Somalia’s semi-autonomous regional administrations, which maintain close ties with Abu Dhabi.

Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, said the UAE’s ties with Somalia would “remain deeper and stronger” despite the president’s criticism.

The diplomatic rupture comes amid an escalating domestic power struggle between Mohamud and regional leaders resisting his efforts to assert federal authority, several of whom have cultivated close ties with Abu Dhabi.

It also marks a striking reversal for a president during whose first term the UAE significantly expanded its foothold in Somalia and who later emerged as one of Abu Dhabi’s strongest defenders.

Somalia’s efforts to rebuild national institutions since the establishment of a permanent federal government in 2012 have unfolded alongside the consolidation of regional administrations that retain considerable autonomy and political power.

Abu Dhabi’s ties with Mogadishu deepened during Mohamud’s first presidency, from 2012 to 2017.

The UAE reopened its embassy in the capital in 2014, and Mohamud inaugurated a UAE-funded military training centre for Somali forces the following year.

At the same time, the Gulf state cultivated commercial, security and diplomatic ties with regional administrations, including Puntland and Jubbaland, as well as Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991.

The UAE is also one of Somalia’s most important trading partners, serving as an important source of imports and a hub for Somali businesses trading in international markets.

But its influence extends well beyond trade, with big investments in infrastructure and security concentrated in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland.

Among the most visible of these investments is Berbera port in Somaliland, where Dubai’s state-owned port operator DP World has invested heavily in expanding the facility and developing a trade corridor connecting it to Ethiopia and the wider region.

Through its subsidiary P&O Ports, the company also operates Bosaso port in Puntland, with both ports providing crucial sources of revenue for their respective administrations.

Somaliland’s Foreign Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adam said the UAE treated it as an independent state, making it an attractive partner, while Emirati investments had created jobs and improved regional connectivity.

“The UAE saw Somaliland’s potential early and backed that view with real investment,” Adam told Al Jazeera.

“The impact on our economy has been significant. DP World’s development of Berbera Port and the Berbera Corridor has turned Berbera into a serious regional gateway,” he added.

Their strategic location along the Gulf of Aden also gives Somaliland and Puntland considerable leverage, making them improtant actors for foreign powers seeking a foothold along one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.

The UAE has developed military facilities near both ports, while in Puntland it helped establish and fund the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF), initially an antipiracy unit that has since become an important counterterrorism force.

More recently, it has supported Puntland’s campaign against ISIL (ISIS) in Somalia with drone attacks and carried out a strike this year against al-Shabab in in October, a security official in the region told Al Jazeera.

Abu Dhabi maintains similar commercial and security ties with Jubbaland, which borders Kenya, although the extent of its involvement there is less publicly documented.

A senior Puntland official speaking anonymously told Al Jazeera the UAE’s interventions had helped regional states consolidate their authority, with no equivalent assistance coming from the federal government. “It is obvious why on that level the UAE is a more important partner,” the official said.

Aweis Ahmed, a Somalia expert at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera that while Emirati support had brought tangible benefits to Somalia’s regional states, it had also strengthened their position against the federal government, leaving the two sides sharply divided over Abu Dhabi’s role.

“They view these things differently. On the one hand, it helps the peripheries, whilst it undermines the centre,” Ahmed said.

That partnership suffered a setback after Mohamud left office in 2017, when his successor, Mohamed Abdullahi, also known as Farmaajo, refused to take sides in a diplomatic dispute between the UAE and Saudi Arabia on one side and Qatar on the other.

The issues escalated sharply in 2018 when Mogadishu rejected a deal involving Dubai’s DP World, Somaliland and Ethiopia over Berbera port, accusing the parties of violating Somalia’s sovereignty.

Relations improved after Mohamud returned to power in 2022, but tensions persisted over Abu Dhabi’s increasingly independent dealings with regional administrations, often bypassing the federal government entirely.

Abdinor Dahir, director of the Somalia-based Adkaysi Institute for Research, Peace and Inclusive Resilience, told Al Jazeera that the UAE’s relationships with regional states had deepened disagreements over who had the authority to conclude agreements with foreign partners.

“Overall, the regional states’ external relationship with the UAE and the resulting disputes weaken federal authority, undermine counterterrorism cooperation, and risk turning foreign policy into a permanent source of internal conflict,” Dahir said.

The dispute came to a head in January, when Mogadishu annulled its agreements with Abu Dhabi, accusing the UAE of secretly transporting an Emirati-backed Yemeni separatist leader through Somaliland without authorisation.

Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland rejected the announcement, insisting their agreements with Abu Dhabi, particularly over ports, would remain in force.

NSA Yusuf Ahmed accused the regional administrations of compromising national security through permitting Emirati control of Somali ports.

“Port agreements for Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, concluded outside federal authority, take strategic infrastructure out of national control,” he said in a post on X. “That is a security question, not a political one.”

But the dispute with the UAE has also become entangled with a wider struggle over political power within Somalia, as Mohamud’s efforts to strengthen the central government through constitutional and electoral changes have met resistance from regional leaders.

Puntland and Jubbaland, both federal member states, have opposed changes they say would weaken their autonomy, while functionally independent Somaliland has long rejected Mogadishu’s authority.

Somali officials have also accused the UAE of backing the deposed leader of Southwest State, Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen, who has fought to retake several towns around the regional capital, Baidoa, in recent months.

Laftagareen told Al Jazeera that he would remove Mohamud’s ally, who took power following a contested election in Baidoa.

Aweis Ahmed, the Chatham House expert, told Al Jazeera the UAE’s support for Mohamud’s domestic opponents had helped them thwart his efforts to push through contentious constitutional and electoral changes.

“This issue with the UAE is more about the local dynamics than some big question about sovereignty for Hassan Sheikh,” he said.

“A direct line to Abu Dhabi gives these sub-national leaders more room to pursue their own priorities when relations with Mogadishu are difficult,” Dahir said.

However, Aweis Ahmed warned that the UAE’s involvement, along with that of other powers from the Middle East, was deepening domestic divisions while drawing Somali actors into wider regional disputes.

“They have made important contributions, but overall their involvement is exacerbating Somalia’s internal and external issues,” he said.

The federal government has aligned itself closely with Turkiye, Qatar and Egypt, while some regional administrations have cultivated ties with the UAE and Ethiopia, and Somaliland has drawn closer to Israel.

“These countries have their own issues, and they’re overlapping with Somalia’s internal rivalries,” Aweis Ahmed said.

At home, Mogadishu has increasingly deployed its growing military strength, including Turkish-trained troops, against UAE-aligned rivals opposed to Mohamud’s constitutional and electoral agenda.

Turkish-trained federal forces helped remove Southwest State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen from power, while a similar attempt to dislodge Jubbaland’s Ahmed Mohamed Islam, also known as Madobe, following his disputed re-election in 2024 failed.

In Puntland, tensions with Mogadishu prompted regional forces to seize several federal military bases and expel federal institutions.

Beyond Somalia, Sudan has complained to Mogadishu about the UAE’s alleged use of facilities in the port cities of Bosaso and Berbera to supply the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting the Sudanese army.

A Somali source told Al Jazeera that Sudan’s intelligence chief raised the issue during a visit to Mogadishu in 2025, pressing Somali officials to at least publicly condemn the alleged supply operations if they were unable to stop them.

In early November, Yassir al-Atta, the Sudanese army chief of staff, went further, alleging that fighters from northern Somalia had taken part in the conflict alongside the RSF.

The passage of Abu Dhabi-backed Yemeni separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi through Somali territory has similarly drawn Mogadishu into tensions between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen.

articles.title: Carving a career from rock pooling passion
articles.summary: Colin Sokel says there is a wonderful world of marine life on our doorstep, and it needs protecting.
articles.body:
"I've been nipped by crabs, pinched by a lobster, bitten by fish and stung by a sea anemone - but that's just part of the game," says Colin Sokell.

He started exploring the Devon coastline at the age of three during angling trips with his grandfather - and a lifelong passion was born.

Sokell now spends hours clambering along Torbay's coast, searching tirelessly for "alien-like" sea hares or cunningly concealed top-knot flat fish.

He shares his encounters with about 130,000 followers on social media: "I was unemployed and thought 'I'm going to be a weirdo and go down to the beach and film what I do' - and it has grown from there."

"I'm going to be an optimist and say next year is the year it's going to be my job," he adds.

Sokell, 32, from Paignton, who takes his children on some of his adventures, tells BBC Radio Devon's John Acres: "Now I've got a platform I can spread conservation awareness and educate people."

Cornwall Wildlife Trust says rock pooling can be a "really positive activity" if you "leave everything as you found it, be respectful and stay safe".

Sokell says people often associate "incredible marine life" with tropical destinations - but encourages them to "appreciate what we have on our doorstep" and "take an interest in protecting it".

His favourite sighting is the sea hare - a type of large, soft-bodied marine snail which looks like a sea slug and gets its name from two ear-like tentacles that sense taste and smell.

"I did a trip on my birthday and found six of them on Torre Abbey Sands," he enthuses.

Sokell is also joyful about crab species: "Brown crabs, European crabs, spider crabs, porcelain crabs, burrowing crabs - you will always find crabs," he adds.

Conger eels, meanwhile, can also be spotted lurking in the shallows.

"People often say they had no idea some of these species are in the UK - I get messages from Canada, Australia, Indonesia - all around the world."

He has even received fan mail from an avid follower in Denmark, he says.

"It's a passion - I just love it," adds Sokel, who has spent decades learning about the marine life he finds.

"It takes me out of reality - it puts me somewhere simple and stress-free. It makes me feel grounded, it's away from tech and screens."

Sokell says he takes the responsibility of his platform seriously - but can still receive negative feedback.

"I don't keep catch or cook any of it - pick it up admire it, talk about it, give a bit of education, and then put it back safely.

"There are mini worlds under each rock and if you leave it upturned it dries out and the creatures die," he adds.

"It can be dangerous depending on the weather and terrain... so I teach young people to be safe doing it."

The marine explorer says he owes much to those early fishing trips "with grandad" which laid the foundation for an interest that has endured nearly three decades.

"People who have watched my videos tell me that they've started looking at the coastline differently, taken their children rock pooling or developed an interest in marine life they never had before.

"In many ways, I hope to pass on that same curiosity and appreciation that my grandad helped instil in me."

Matt Slater, marine conservation officer at Cornwall Wildlife Trust, said rock pooling was a "really positive activity if done well".

It is an activity often associated with warm, long summer's days, but winter rock poolers can find colourful nudibranch (a type of sea slug), crab species - including the mongaus -and the cushion starfish, he said.

Conger eels, sea hares and top-knot flat fish are also still around, while Slater said the most colourful sight on a grey day is likely to be the rainbow sea slug.

"You have to be respectful to the wildlife you encounter and leave it as you find it and keep safe."

He said it was vital to always put rocks back how you find them - the same way up - while handling animals carefully and not "overcrowding buckets".

While winter was a great time to explore rock pools - he recommended staying away from areas on the northern and western coasts exposed to surf due to increased danger as well as fewer rock pooling opportunities.

"Places like Falmouth and within the estuary there, you can find amazing rock pooling at this time of year," he added.

articles.title: A homeless Marine veteran in Colorado Springs received an unexpected gift from local support groups: a donated car he says will help him reach medical appointments and search for an apartment as he rebuilds his life
articles.summary: A donated car has given a 68-year-old Marine Corps veteran in Colorado Springs a chance to regain some independence after months of homelessness and
articles.body: A donated car has given a 68-year-old Marine Corps veteran in Colorado Springs a chance to regain some independence after months of homelessness and health difficulties. Thurman “Hank” Jones Jr. received a car from Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center and medical transport company MedRide on Thursday. He hopes to use it to attend medical appointments, find affordable accommodation and look for employment.Jones had been without a vehicle after the one he previously owned broke down. The loss made an already difficult situation harder, as he was also dealing with cancer and had been living without a permanent home. His new car came through efforts by people who learnt about his circumstances and decided to help him.The donation was made possible through cooperation between local organisations. KRDO reported that several groups had spent weeks arranging the vehicle for Jones. According to The Gazette, the effort began after Bob McLaughlin, executive director of Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center, learnt that the veteran needed transport.For Jones, the gift addresses a practical problem that had affected several parts of his daily life. He can now travel for medical care and explore housing options instead of having to manage these journeys on foot. He also hopes the vehicle will help him and his dog, Dottie, as they try to move towards a more stable situation.When Jones lost his carJones' housing problems began about eight months before the car was donated. He was evicted from his residence and subsequently stayed in his vehicle with Dottie.That arrangement did not last. When the car stopped working, Jones had to sell it. A city ordinance prohibited people from living in their vehicles, a practice known as vehicle camping. Losing the car therefore left him without both a place to stay and a means of getting around.Travelling through Colorado Springs was particularly difficult without personal transport. The city has hilly terrain, making it harder for Jones to cover distances on foot. He spoke about the difficulty of navigating the area at his age.“There’s nothing flat in this town,” Jones told The Gazette, explaining that getting around on foot had become difficult.His health concerns added to the challenges. The veteran had been dealing with cancer and needed a reliable way to reach medical appointments. Without a vehicle, even routine travel had become a concern.Jones also wanted to find another place to live. Having transport would allow him to visit apartments, compare what he could afford and take steps towards leaving homelessness behind.How the community arranged the carThe effort to find a vehicle began after Jones spoke to McLaughlin about the problems he was facing. The Mt. Carmel executive director knew the veteran and understood that the absence of transport was affecting his ability to manage everyday needs.McLaughlin decided to approach people in the community to see whether someone could help. His search led to a meeting with Tyler Borzileri of MedRide in Pueblo about three weeks before the car was handed over.During their conversation, McLaughlin mentioned that a veteran needed a vehicle. Borzileri said the medical transport company had one it could donate.The organisation then prepared the car before transferring it to Jones. MedRide technicians removed the company's branding from the sedan, cleaned it inside and outside, and carried out a tune-up. The vehicle had previously been used for the company's transport operations.Borzileri assured Jones that the car had been refurbished and was in good condition before handing him the keys.The presentation took place at Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center on November 19. Jones appeared overwhelmed when he saw the vehicle and was initially unable to say much about the gesture.What the car means for Jones and his dogThe new car is expected to make it easier for Jones to attend medical appointments, travel around Colorado Springs and look for work. It will also give him the flexibility to visit potential apartments and assess housing options.After receiving the keys, Jones said he planned to visit the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) first to complete the necessary formalities to make the vehicle road legal. He also intended to meet a close friend who had supported him during difficult periods.Dottie, his dog, will also benefit from having a way to travel with him. The two had been living together in his car after he lost his residence, before the vehicle broke down.Jones said the support had affected him emotionally as well as practically. His circumstances had sometimes made him feel that he was not worthy of receiving help. The donation changed that feeling.He described the gesture as something that had made him feel valued during a difficult period. He also expressed gratitude towards the people and organisations that had stepped in to help.Jones said he had lived in different parts of the country but had not experienced the same kind of community support he found in Colorado Springs. He particularly appreciated the people at Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center.The donated car does not resolve all the difficulties Jones faces, including his housing and health concerns. However, it gives him a way to deal with some immediate challenges and pursue the next steps towards greater independence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
articles.summary: Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the
articles.body: Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks. It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2012, Thai engineers embedded geotextile and geogrid in a Highway 11 test section; the best layout recorded 11 mm of rutting after 80 wheel passes, versus 17 mm in the control
articles.summary: Discover how innovative geotextile and geogrid reinforcements on Thailand's Highway 11 significantly reduced rutting, improving road safety and longevity. Research highlights optimal placement for maximum benefits.
articles.body: Heavy traffic can gradually damage asphalt roads, leaving grooves where vehicle tyres repeatedly pass over the same area. These depressions, known as ruts, can affect driving comfort, drainage and road safety. In Thailand, researchers tested whether embedding geosynthetic materials inside pavement layers could help roads withstand repeated traffic loads. This study was conducted using a large-scale trial on Highway 11, Uttaradit Province. In February 2012, four sections of road pavement were constructed, comprising three reinforced sections and one non-reinforced section. This study revealed that the use of geotextile and geogrid at various depths of the road pavement increased resistance to rutting.Four pavement sections tested on Highway 11The research was led by Thanongsak Imjai, Kypros Pilakoutas and Maurizio Guadagnini. Their initial findings appeared in a 2015 paper, "Advanced Geosynthetics in Flexible Pavement: A Full-Scale Test and Numerical Study", published through the University of Sheffield Engineering Symposium. The team made four testing sections, each one of 50 m, between kilometre points 102+700 and 102+900. Three sections were reinforced using geosynthetics, while the fourth section, named P1, acted as the control section without reinforcement. Two materials were used for testing. Geotextiles are permeable textile-type materials that are used to separate soils and aggregates. Geogrids are a type of material that is used to stabilise aggregates. Every testing section has its own arrangement of geosynthetic material. In the case of the P4 section, there was paving fabric near the top of the base layer and the geogrid below the base but near the sub-base layer.Early loading tests showed lower ruttingThe researchers utilised 20-tonne, 30-tonne and 40-tonne trucks to investigate the reaction of the pavement sections to the applied loads. They also attached sensors for measuring the deformation and stress experienced by the road construction. According to the 2015 University of Sheffield Engineering Symposium paper, section P4 recorded a maximum rut depth of 11 mm after 36 months of service. The unreinforced control section, P1, recorded a maximum rut depth of 17 mm over the same 36 months, the paper reports. P4 also did better than the other two reinforced sections, P2 and P3, which recorded 17 mm and 18 mm in the same paper. These readings were taken after three years of service on the highway.Longer monitoring confirmed the benefits of reinforcementIn the second study titled "Performance of Geosynthetic-Reinforced Flexible Pavements in Full-Scale Field Trials", which appeared in the journal Geotextiles and Geomembranes in April 2019, the investigators observed the four sections for around 60 months. Maximum surface rut depth ranged from 17 to 23 mm in the four sections investigated. The section without reinforcement suffered the highest surface deformation, while the reinforced sections resisted rutting better than the unreinforced control. Section P4, which used the geotextile and geogrid, was the most resistant to rutting.Additionally, the investigators made comparisons between observations made in the field and the predictions generated using a numerical model created by the University of Sheffield. This study indicates that geosynthetic material could be helpful in enhancing the performance of flexible pavements and preventing deformation as a result of vehicle traffic. Moreover, the study highlights the importance of positioning the reinforcement appropriately. Although the study took place on a single highway, it provides important information for engineers. The findings also suggest that the effectiveness of geosynthetic reinforcement depends on how it is placed within a pavement layers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page says she nearly messed up Gavin and Stacey audition
articles.summary: The Swansea actress says she was told her Cardiff accent sounded "awful".
articles.body:
Joanna Page has said she nearly messed up her Gavin And Stacey audition after failing to do a Cardiff accent.

The 49-year-old rose to fame after starring as Stacey in the BBC comedy opposite creators James Corden and Ruth Jones.

Page, from Swansea, told campmates on ITV's I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! that she had initially read some scenes for Jones using her actual accent.

She recounted that she was then asked to do it in a Cardiff accent, as that was where her character was supposed to be from, but Jones told her it sounded "awful" and to "just be you".

Speaking about her preparations for the life-changing audition, she said: "I remember reading the script, Ruth and James had written it and I remember thinking, 'This is me, she is me, I can do this'."

Page said she got the offer for the part in the Bafta-winning sitcom two weeks after being rejected from a West End show.

She said: "I was working in a shoe shop in East Dulwich and I'd just missed out on getting the part in Dirty Dancing The Musical.

"And so if I'd have got that, I never, ever would have done it."

Page also recalled her first impression of Mathew Horne – who played Gavin in the series – during their chemistry read and said "he seemed really cool, and I thought I'm not cool and I'm just a nerd".

The hit series aired for three seasons from 2007 until 2009 followed by Christmas specials including the series finale in 2024.

Page's autobiography, entitled Lush, recounts her youth in a small village near Swansea , graduating from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada) and early stage and screen performances before her big break in Gavin and Stacey.

Her TV and film credits include romantic comedy Love Actually, Nativity 2: Danger in the Manger and Doctor Who, where she played Queen Elizabeth I in The Day of the Doctor, and she also does presenting and podcasting.

articles.title: Companies diverted Trump's $100bn tariff refunds to bonuses, not consumers: Report
articles.summary: Several companies that received refunds for tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump have directed some of the money towards corporate bonuses rather
articles.body: Several companies that received refunds for tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump have directed some of the money towards corporate bonuses rather than reimbursing consumers, according to a report.After examining securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies that disclosed receiving tariff refunds and indicated that some of the money would go towards compensation for their leadership, The Guardian reported.Toolmaker Stanley Black & Decker, which makes products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, had told consumers that it was forced to raise prices because of Trump's import fees. The company is expected to receive at least $298 million in tariff refunds and indicated that part of the amount would go towards bonuses, according to ProPublica.Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, both owned by parent company TJX, also indicated that tariff refunds would contribute to employee bonuses. A TJX spokesperson confirmed that the company had received a total of $331 million in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered by the Supreme Court ruling.The spokesperson said the refunds had resulted in “incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”. The company added that it had not disclosed a further breakdown because the amount was still an accrual and its current financial year had not ended.In its financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, ProPublica reported. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The Trump administration has refunded at least $100 billion to companies since August, accounting for about 60 per cent of the roughly $165 billion collected in tariffs. The refunds followed a Supreme Court ruling that Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs were unlawful because they exceeded his executive authority and required congressional approval.Some companies immediately sued the US government seeking refunds after the ruling. Trump, however, said he would “remember” which companies sought reimbursements and praised those that held off. The administration has not disclosed which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.While several companies had said they increased prices because of tariffs, it has largely remained unclear how they intend to use the reimbursements. ProPublica found that most companies publicly committing to refund customers were those dealing directly with other businesses rather than consumers. Others have remained vague about whether they would use the money to lower prices or avoid future increases.Research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimated that 26 per cent of tariff increases are passed on to consumer prices, while the Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost US households around $900 annually under current laws.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Canadian homebuyer agreed to pay over $1 million for a pre-construction condo but couldn't secure a mortgage; builder resold the unit for $699,900, yet court ordered it to return his $121,098 deposit with interest
articles.summary: A Canadian homebuyer who could not secure a mortgage for a pre-construction condominium in Ontario has won a court battle to recover his $121,098 deposit,
articles.body: A Canadian homebuyer who could not secure a mortgage for a pre-construction condominium in Ontario has won a court battle to recover his $121,098 deposit, despite the builder reselling the property for considerably less than the original purchase price. The Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruled that the purchase agreement was not binding because the developer could not prove it had delivered a legally required condominium buyers’ guide. The March 2026 decision also awarded the buyer interest on his deposit and $31,000 towards his legal costs.Court orders builder to return $121,098 condo depositThe dispute involved a pre-construction condominium in Hamilton, Ontario, which the buyer agreed to purchase in March 2022 for just over $1 million. According to the ‘Money,’ the buyer paid a total deposit of $121,098 towards the property.However, when the transaction reached its closing stage in February 2024, he was unable to secure the financing needed to complete the purchase. The sale consequently fell through, leaving the builder with a unit it needed to sell again.The developer subsequently resold the condominium for $699,900, substantially below the original agreed price. The difference was approximately $300,000, creating a significant financial dispute between the two parties.The builder sought to retain the buyer’s deposit and also to recover other losses resulting from the lower resale price and costs of holding the property. But the buyer challenged the contract itself, arguing that the developer had not fulfilled an important legal prerequisite before the sale.As explained by Lumen LLP, the buyer argued that the purchase agreement had never become legally binding because he had not received Ontario's required Residential Condominium Buyers' Guide.What does Ontario law require from condominium buildersThe central issue in the case was the documents that developers are legally required to provide when selling new condominium units.In Ontario, the Condominium Act, 1998 requires that developers provide buyers with two important documents; the Residential Condominium Buyers’ Guide and the most current disclosure statement. These documents explain the buying process, and the rights and risks of a purchaser in buying a property before it is constructed.According to the case analysis of Lumen LLP, developers have been required to provide the disclosure statement with the condominium guide as of January 1, 2021, pursuant to Section 72(1) of the Act. Furthermore, section 72(2) provides that a purchase agreement shall not be binding on the buyer unless both documents have been delivered.The legislation also gives buyers a 10-day cooling-off period in which to cancel the agreement without a financial penalty. But the signing of the contract does not automatically start this period.The Condominium Authority of Ontario says the 10 days don’t start until the purchaser has received all three documents: the buyers’ guide, the latest disclosure statement and a copy of the purchase agreement signed by both the buyer and developer. If the buyer cancels within this period, the developer is obliged to return the deposit immediately, plus any interest earned.The builder's electronic acknowledgment failedThe developer attempted to defend its position by relying on an electronic acknowledgment included in the purchase agreement. The document carried the buyer's electronic signature and indicated that he had received the condominium guide.However, the court was not convinced that this acknowledgment established actual delivery. According to Lumen LLP, the same acknowledgment also confirmed that the buyer had received a fully signed purchase agreement and the disclosure statement. Evidence suggested that he could not have received those documents on the date he signed the acknowledgment.The builder was able to produce records showing when certain other documents had been emailed to the purchaser. However, it could not provide comparable evidence showing when or how the condominium guide had been sent.This distinction became central to the case. A signed acknowledgment was not sufficient evidence of actual receipt of the document as required by law.The developer could not prove delivery of the guide, the court held. Therefore, the agreement had never been binding on the purchaser and the 10-day cancellation period had not been triggered.The March 2026 ruling went beyond the deposit disputeThe Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruled in the buyer’s favor in March 2026. The developer was ordered to repay the full deposit of $121,098 plus interest.The builder also claimed further damages in relation to the resale of the condominium and carrying costs associated with it. The court dismissed this claim too. The buyer also was awarded $31,000 in legal fees.The builder also argued that the buyer's actions, including paying deposits and signing amendments to the agreement, meant he had accepted the contract. The court rejected this position.What the decision means for other pre-construction buyersThe judgment could be important for other Ontario homebuyers who find themselves unable to complete pre-construction purchases. However, it does not mean that anyone who fails to obtain a mortgage can automatically walk away from a condominium agreement and recover their deposit.‘Money’ reported that the outcome depended on the builder's failure to establish that it had fulfilled its legal disclosure obligations. The distinction matters because financing difficulties alone are not a valid reason to cancel an otherwise binding purchase agreement.Lumen LLP also referenced a prior case, Chen v. Brookfield Residential (Ontario) Limited, 2022 ONCA 887, in which a buyer who received a low appraisal of the property attempted to back out of a purchase. The court held that the buyer's notice of cancellation was void and that he was in breach of the agreement. Buyers are at risk of losing their deposits and being held liable for the developer’s loss on resale.The Condominium Authority of Ontario recommends that purchasers maintain written records of every document received during the buying process.You use AI every day. articles.title: Illegal immigrant avoids charges after Florida grandmother killed outside grocery store, enraging family
articles.summary: Prosecutors dropped all charges against Carlos Suarez-Contreras in Deborah Murphy's death at a Panama City Beach Publix, citing hurdles under Florida law.
articles.body: The criminal case against an illegal immigrant accused of backing over and killing an elderly woman in a grocery store parking lot has been dismissed. He will not face any charges for the accident, Larry Basford, state attorney for Florida’s Fourteenth Judicial Circuit, told Fox News Digital. Several factors prevented prosecutors from pursuing and securing charges under Florida law, Basford said. ‘VIBRANT’ FLORIDA GRANDMA ALLEGEDLY KILLED BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT OUTSIDE PUBLIX, FAMILY FIGHTS FOR JUSTICE "I think everyone would agree that what he did was careless and it was negligent," Basford said. But, "not every tragedy amounts to a crime." That’s heartbreaking news for the family of 82-year-old Deborah Murphy, said Murphy’s daughter, Amy Edge. Both sets of tires crushed her body before the car stopped, she and her twin sister Beth Schulz told Fox News Digital. THREE-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH KILLING NORTH CAROLINA GIRL, 6, AFTER RUNNING STOP SIGN On May 17, Murphy walked back to her car carrying a bag after a brief stop at Publix in Panama City Beach. Surveillance video shows her striding through the crosswalk toward her car, when she was struck by a Toyota 4Runner moving in reverse, according to court records. She was facing away from the vehicle as she walked, the video shows. She apparently didn’t see it coming. FLORIDA DMV WORKER FACES 360 FELONIES FOR ALLEGEDLY HELPING ILLEGAL ALIENS GET LICENSES WITHOUT DRIVING TESTS The driver, Carlos Suarez-Contreras, was a 26-year-old from Venezuela who was in the United States illegally, arrest records show. He was driving the vehicle with a canceled Georgia license, arrest records show. Murphy was pushed to the ground by the SUV. But it didn’t stop. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCKER CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, 2 YOUNG SONS HEADING TO AIRPORT The car continued backing up, "running over Ms. Murphy," according to an arrest affidavit submitted by the Florida Highway Patrol. Suarez-Contreras was charged with driving with a canceled license and causing a death, a third-degree felony. ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER He was held without bond because of his immigration status and because he was thought to be a "potential flight risk," Florida Highway Patrol records show. Murphy was taken to the hospital and died from blunt force injuries less than an hour later, her daughters said. Prosecutors worked on the case for almost six months, searching for answers that could lead to a conviction. "We tried not to leave any stone unturned," Basford said. ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’ They found that Suarez-Contreras’ driver’s license had been canceled. But it became invalid only a day before the accident. The Georgia Department of Driver Services confirmed to Fox News Digital that Suarez-Contreras' license had been canceled. Citing privacy concerns, an agency spokeswoman would not say when it had been canceled, or when he would have been notified. A non-U.S. citizen establishing residency in Georgia "must obtain a Georgia driver’s license within 30 days," according to the Georgia Department of Driver Services website. A non-U.S. citizen is considered a resident if he or she "accepts employment or engages in trade in Georgia, and enrolls his or her children in a private or public school within ten days after the commencement of employment," according to the agency. A person can also be considered a "resident" of Georgia if he or she is "present in the state for 30 or more days." Prosecutor’s dilemma The question of whether Suarez-Contreras knew the license had been canceled is what proved problematic for prosecutors in Florida. "Under the law, we have to prove that the individual knew his license was suspended," Basford said. Prosecutors considered charging him with vehicular homicide and manslaughter, Basford said. But they couldn’t establish the culpable negligence needed for that. Using the surveillance video that captured the fatal accident, investigators re-enacted the scene. Considering that information, they decided the SUV wasn’t backing quickly enough to prove Suarez-Contreras was driving "recklessly" when he drove over Murphy. At the scene, the passenger of the car, Luis Sanabria, gave sworn testimony to a law enforcement officer that it was Suarez-Contreras who "was operating the vehicle at the time of the crash." Sanabria was found to have an expired visa, according to the incident report. He was released into the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Jacob Navarro, public affairs specialist for the Bay County Sheriff’s Office, told Fox News Digital. In considering charges for Suarez-Contreras, prosecutors looked to a Florida law passed in 2023. It invalidates a driver’s license issued to an illegal immigrant in certain states, such as California, Connecticut and Delaware. Unfortunately, the legislation does not designate Georgia as one of "those liberal states that gave licenses out so freely to individuals," Basford said. Murphy’s family is devastated that there’s no chance of justice, Edge said. "We feel incredibly let down by the state of Florida, who vowed to seek justice on her behalf," she said. "It's like experiencing the loss all over again." Murphy was in great health and presumably had many more years with the family, Edge said.Now, she won't attend her grandchildren’s weddings, or meet any more of her great-grandchildren, she said. "That's been taken away." Fighting for change Murphy’s two daughters are incredulous that Florida isn’t pursuing a trial. It could have set a new precedent for this type of case, Edge said. At the beginning of the investigation the prosecution team had been very optimistic about securing multiple charges for Suarez-Contreras, she said. The only question in their minds at the time was the length of the prison sentence he would receive if convicted, she said. She and her sister question the way their mother’s death was investigated and why so much weight was given to a re-enactment of the incident. "We know the man killed her," Edge said. "He never got out of the car. He never ran to her aid. He never stopped. He wasn't reversing from a spot. He drove backwards." The family also questions why Suarez-Contreras wasn’t tested for drugs or alcohol and why his phone records weren’t reviewed. Yet, Murphy’s body was subjected to a toxicology evaluation, her daughters said. The sisters will continue to fight to bring positive changes from the tragedy. They may pursue changes to Florida law or the way law enforcement officers conduct similar investigations. SEND US A TIP "There's a lot of different questions we have that we'll continue to explore, but not in a vengeful way," Edge said. It’s "more in that we don't want this to happen to someone else." GOT A TIP? There’s some comfort knowing Suarez-Contreras is in ICE custody awaiting deportation, she said. "We don't want him to be able to do this to anyone else in the United States. Our drive now is to ensure that he is deported." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Suarez-Contreras’ defense attorney, Russell Ramey, told Fox News Digital that he’s pleased the charges were dropped. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP After the case was dropped, Suarez-Contreras was transferred into ICE custody on Nov. 15, according to the Bay County Jail. Fox News Digital could not reach him for comment.

articles.body: Dumka: Five persons were arrested for intimidating rivals using bouncers to settle a land dispute at Simladhab village under Barhait police station limits in Sahibganj district on Nov 17. Among the accused are the owner of a bouncer agency, a bouncer and three others, police said on Sunday.Barharwa sub-divisional police officer (SDPO) Nitin Khandelwal a dispute over a plot of land broke out between two groups on Nov 17. A video of the alleged assault by bouncers went viral on social media. Later a complaint was registered at Barhait police station against five named and 10 unidentified persons by Mohan Soren. Sahibganj SP Amit Kumar Singh then formed a special investigation team led by Khandelwal to probe the incident.Khandelwal said a raid was carried out at Simaldhab village on Nov 20 after receiving reports that bouncers had reached the village again. Shivam Kumar, the owner of the agency and Anil Kumar Mishra, a bouncer, were arrested. Three others, Piyush Kumar, Lalan Kumar Singh and Sudhanshu Ranjan, were arrested later.During interrogation, Shivam informed the police that John Chunda Hansda, a native of the village who is currently posted at the public works department in Chatra, had reached out to him seeking bouncers to help take possession of his ancestral land. “Shivam reached the village with bouncers on Nov 17 but fled after coming to know that police were approaching,” Khandelwal said.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news.
